claims.claim: Planar two-exit instances admit a cyclic two-gate decomposition. Let the exits be p,q and let B=N(p)∩N(q). Every component of G−({p,q}∪B) is adjacent to at most two vertices of B; when |B|≥3, those two are consecutive in the cyclic order of B around the exits.
claims.evidence: For |B|≥3, the embedded K_{2,|B|} skeleton is 2-connected. Euler's formula gives exactly |B| faces, while bipartiteness and simplicity make every facial boundary have length at least four. Since the total facial-boundary length is 4|B|, every face is a 4-cycle p-b_i-q-b_{i+1}-p. The drawing of any connected component disjoint from the skeleton lies in one face, so its B-neighbors are among that face's two consecutive gates. For |B|≤2, the cardinality bound is immediate.
claims.search_method: Independent planar-embedding and face-count proof, supplemented by the K_{3,3}-minor obstruction obtained by contracting any component meeting three gates.

claims.claim: There is a linear-time classification when the exits have the same independent neighborhood. After deleting a possible irrelevant edge pq, suppose N(p)=N(q)=B and B is independent. The fugitive wins exactly when (i) s∈{p,q}∪B, (ii) s has a neighbor in B, or (iii) s has a neighbor w having two distinct neighbors in B.
claims.evidence: The three positive cases have direct winning strategies. Conversely, after the first move, the containing outside component has at most two boundary gates. Negating (ii) and (iii) leaves at most one gate adjacent to the new position, so Nemesis deletes one exit edge at that gate and can similarly damage the other boundary gate before it is entered. Upon entry into a damaged gate she deletes its second exit edge. Because B is independent, leaving this dead gate requires entering an outside component whose boundary already contains it and therefore has at most one new gate; Nemesis damages that gate before the next move. This invariant prevents entry into any gate with two intact exit edges, and finite edge deletion ensures eventual loss. The B=∅ case is immediate. Membership and relevant gate-neighbor counts are computable by adjacency scans. A fresh bounded search found no discrepancy in 19,252 graph/start pairs.
claims.search_method: Invariant proof plus exhaustive integer edge-mask minimax over all labeled instances with 1–3 gates and 0–3 outside vertices satisfying the two-gate component property.

claims.claim: Two broader target-relevant subclasses are linearly solvable: (a) the graph induced by regular vertices is a forest, with arbitrary degrees; or (b) every regular vertex has degree at most three, with arbitrary exit degrees.
claims.evidence: Handle starts already at exits immediately, discard the irrelevant exit-exit edge, and replace every regular-to-exit incidence by an edge to its own fresh leaf exit. Regular positions and relevant edges then correspond bijectively; reaching or remaining connected to an original exit is equivalent to reaching or remaining connected to a corresponding leaf. Thus outcomes are preserved. In case (a), every transformed starting component is a tree. In case (b), the transformed graph has maximum degree at most three. The authorized source's linear-time theorem for trees and maximum-degree-three simple graphs applies, and the transformation has linear size. Exhaustive exact comparison confirmed splitting preservation on 3,208 small graph/start instances, including 548 graphs containing the discarded exit-exit edge.
claims.search_method: Outcome-preserving reduction proof plus exhaustive integer-mask comparison before and after exit splitting for every simple labeled graph on 3–5 vertices with two fixed exits and every regular start.

claims.claim: The binary-escape-tree condition is not necessary even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. A seven-vertex counterexample has exits p,q, start s, regular vertices a,b,c,z, and edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ab,az,bz,bc,cz,cs.
claims.evidence: An exact noncrossing integral straight-line drawing certifies planarity, and full edge-mask minimax returns a fugitive win. After s→c, deletion of bc is answered by c→z; the edge-disjoint configurations {za,ap,aq} and {zb,bp,bq} ensure one remains intact after the next deletion. Any other first deletion leaves c→b; a surviving b-exit edge wins immediately, while deletion of both b-exit edges leaves ab,ap,aq intact enough to win through a. After exit splitting, only s and c are within distance one of s. Vertex s has degree one. A binary tree rooted at c must use children b and z, after which z must use a and the already-used b, impossible in a tree. Exhaustive search rejected all 2,046 rooted edge-subset candidates.
claims.witness: The claimed seven-vertex graph with integral drawing a=(0,0), b=(120,0), p=(60,80), q=(60,-80), z=(60,40), c=(90,10), s=(80,23).
claims.search_method: Exact integer segment-intersection certification, exhaustive integer edge-mask minimax, and exhaustive binary-tree edge-subset search for roots s and c.

claims.claim: An exact recurrence gives PSPACE membership and an O*(8^n) planar algorithm, although not a polynomial classification. For deleted-edge set D and current regular vertex v, W(D,v) holds iff some surviving move vw reaches an exit or, for every surviving edge e Nemesis might delete, w remains connected to an exit and W(D∪{e},w) holds.
claims.evidence: Under the natural binding W(D,v)=∃vw∉D [w is an exit ∨ ∀e∉D (w remains exit-connected in G−(D∪{e}) and W(D∪{e},w))], the quantifiers exactly match Fugitive-then-Nemesis play. Each recursive call adds an edge to D, so the recurrence is acyclic. There are at most n·2^m states with polynomial transition work. For planar simple graphs with n≥3, m≤3n−6, yielding O*(2^m)=O*(8^n); smaller cases are constant. Depth-first evaluation has polynomial depth and polynomial-size frames, proving PSPACE membership. A separate explicit alternating-turn evaluator agreed with the recurrence on all 3,208 tested small graph/start instances.
claims.search_method: Direct quantified-game proof plus exhaustive comparison of independent deleted-mask and remaining-mask evaluators over every simple labeled graph on 3–5 vertices with fixed exits and every regular start.

target_evidence: All five claims survive audit and provide material structural information, exact linear-time subclasses, a genuine counterexample to necessity of the binary-escape-tree condition, and an exponential upper bound. They do not provide either a polynomial-time algorithm for all planar simple graphs with exactly two exits or a matching hardness result, which is the exact requested target. The final writeup explicitly calls the result partial and disclaims both full alternatives, so claimed_resolution PARTIAL is accurate.
